title: The Nile year
subtitle: Three seasons as a working lens, not a calendar you could set a watch by
question: How did the river's year organise labour, institutions, and religious attention?
period: Pharaonic Egypt broadly; the pattern is a long-term structure rather than a dated event
evidenceBoundary: Akhet, Peret, and Shemu are an Egyptian administrative and agricultural scheme. Flood height and timing varied year to year, a bad flood meant famine, and the civil calendar drifted against the actual river. Modern dams have ended the annual inundation entirely, so no living observation can stand in for it.
reconstruction: Season names and their agricultural content come from the archive's geography and chronology material. Labour details are the general pattern described there, not a record of any one village's year.
accessibleSummary: Three seasons in order, each with its approximate months, river state, agricultural work, and religious associations, given as text.

scenes.title: Akhet — inundation
scenes.body: Floodwater covered the fields and left silt behind. Fields could not be worked, so labour moved to repair, transport, construction, and institutional service. Hapi, the personified inundation, is shown heavy-bodied with aquatic plants, binding the Two Lands together.
detail: A high flood destroyed; a low flood starved. Neither was rare.
Egyptians associated the water's origin with caverns near the First Cataract.

scenes.title: Peret — emergence
scenes.body: As the water fell, land came back out and was sown. Boundaries had to be re-established, canals maintained, and assessments made. Emergence is also the vocabulary of creation: land appearing out of water is the founding image of the whole system.
detail: The same word family describes the primeval mound rising from Nun.
Osiris festivals in this part of the year tie germination to regeneration.

scenes.title: Shemu — harvest and low water
scenes.body: Grain was reaped, threshed, measured, and stored. Measurement is a religious act here as much as an economic one: assessment, taxation, and temple provisioning all run through it. Then the river dropped to its lowest and the year waited.
detail: Temple estates were provisioned from this cycle.
The waiting is the point: the flood's return was needed, not guaranteed.

scenes.title: The river's own inhabitants
scenes.body: Sobek is a crocodile in a river that had crocodiles in it. He carries water, fertility, aggression, and royal power at once, and his cult concentrates where the water spreads out — the Fayum marshes and, later, Kom Ombo.
detail: The Fayum's Middle Kingdom royal patronage is the clearest case of ecology and politics arriving together.

scenes.title: What ended
scenes.body: The annual inundation no longer happens. Dam construction in the twentieth century replaced it with managed release. Anything you can watch on the river today is a modern hydrological system, and this journey is a reconstruction of a vanished one.
detail: This is stated here so that no image or footage in the archive is mistaken for the ancient cycle.
